items.prose: Four pirates share 100 coins. The most senior proposes, and everyone aboard votes, proposer included. At least half yes passes it; otherwise he goes overboard. Each wants to survive, then coins, then to see others thrown over.
items.question: How many coins does the proposer keep?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work up from 2 aboard and buy the cheapest vote.

byKey.hundred: He needs one vote besides his own. Nobody votes yes for 0 when they would get 0 anyway.
byKey.twentyfive: An equal split loses the second pirate's vote and wastes coins.
byKey.ninetyeight: Two votes of four is half, so he buys one, not two.

explain.text: With 3 aboard the split is (99, 0, 1), so the third pirate of four gets 0 there. One coin buys him, and the proposer keeps 99. Principle: price each vote by the next game.

items.prose: Ten people stand in a line, each seeing every hat in front. Hats come in three colours. They call from the back and may agree a code first.
items.question: How many can a code guarantee?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One call can carry the sum modulo 3.

byKey.ten: The back person has no information about his own hat.
byKey.three: That is about a third of 10, the rate for random guesses, which guarantee nobody.
byKey.eight: One call is enough: the sum of what he sees modulo 3.

explain.text: Number the colours 0, 1 and 2. The back person calls the sum he sees modulo 3, and each other person subtracts what they see and hear. So 9 are certain.

items.prose: Twelve prisoners each open 6 of 12 boxes, following the numbers from their own box.
items.question: What is the team's chance of success?

byKey.fail: That is the chance of a cycle longer than 6.

explain.text: The team fails when a cycle of length 7 to 12 exists, chance $1/7 + \cdots + 1/12 \approx 0.6532$. Success is $1 - 0.6532 = 0.3468$. At most one such cycle exists, so the chances add.

items.prose: Two eggs and 80 floors. An egg breaks from some floor upwards, possibly none.
items.question: What is the fewest drops that always finds that floor?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest $d$ with $d(d+1)/2 \ge 80$.

byKey.seven: That is binary search, which two eggs cannot sustain.
byKey.nine: $\sqrt{80} \approx 9$ is the every-$k$-floors idea, which wastes drops.

explain.text: $12 \cdot 13/2 = 78$ falls short of 80 and $13 \cdot 14/2 = 91$ covers it. So 13 drops, first from floor 13. Principle: invert the triangle numbers.

items.prose: Six children, four of them muddy. The teacher says that at least one of them is muddy, then asks each round who knows.
items.question: In which round do the muddy children step forward?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $k$ muddy they act in round $k$.

byKey.three: Each sees 3 muddy faces and must watch round 3 pass in silence.
byKey.one: Each sees muddy faces, so nobody is sure in round 1.

explain.text: Each muddy child sees 3 muddy faces and waits to see if those 3 act in round 3. They do not, so all four act in round 4. The clean children never step forward.

items.prose: Four people cross a bridge for two at night with one torch. They take 1, 2, 4 and 9 minutes; a pair walks at the slower pace.
items.question: What is the fewest minutes?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $2b$ with $a + y$.

byKey.escort: Escorting costs $2 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 9 = 17$. Shuttling is cheaper here.
byKey.fifteen: That adds 2, 4 and 9 with no returns; the torch must come back twice.

explain.text: $2b = 4$ is less than $a + y = 5$, so shuttle: $2 + 1 + 9 + 2 + 2 = 16$. Escorting costs 17. A search over every plan confirms 16.

items.prose: Twelve lions and one sheep. A lion that eats the sheep falls asleep and becomes a sheep. Every lion would rather live than eat, but eats whenever it is safe.
items.question: Does the first lion eat the sheep?

options.why: If it eats, 11 lions are awake, and an odd number eats the sleeper.

options.text: Only if no other lion is near
options.why: Every lion reasons the same way; only the count decides.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the lions left awake after an eater falls asleep.

byKey.yes: Eating leaves 11 awake, and 11 is odd, so one of them eats the sleeper.
byKey.sometimes: Parity of the count decides, not position.

explain.text: With $n$ lions the first eats exactly when $n$ is odd. Twelve is even, so eating would leave 11 hungry lions and a sleeping sheep. The first lion waits.

items.prose: Six people, red and blue hats, calling from the back. The code: the back person says blue if he sees an even number of reds.

state.caption: Hats from the front, person 6 at the back.

items.question: What does each person call?

feedback.correct: B from the back, then B, B, B, R, R.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The back person follows the code; the others name their own hats.

byKey.r0c1: Person 6 sees 2 reds, an even number, so he says blue.
byKey.r1c1: Person 5 sees 2 reds and heard 'even', so his own hat is blue.

explain.text: Person 6 sees two reds, an even count, so he says blue, wrong for his own red hat. Each of the others counts reds in front plus reds called behind. All five are right.

items.prose: Ten prisoners each open 5 of 10 boxes, following the numbers from their own box.
items.question: What is prisoner 1's own chance of finding his number?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. His cycle length is equally likely to be 1 to 10.

byKey.team: That is the chance that all ten succeed.

explain.text: The cycle through box 1 has each length from 1 to 10 with chance $1/10$. He succeeds when it is at most 5, chance $5/10 = 0.5$. Only the joint chance changes under the strategy.

items.prose: Three logicians are asked whether everyone wants a coffee. The first two each say 'I don't know'. The third does not want one.
items.question: What does the third say?

options.why: She knows her own wish, and that settles the question.
The first two want one, but she does not, so not everyone does.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Her own wish settles an 'everyone' question.

byKey.idk: She has the last piece of information: her own answer is no.
byKey.yes: Each 'I don't know' means yes for that speaker, but she does not want one.

explain.text: Each 'I don't know' means the speaker wants a coffee. The third does not, so not everyone does. She says no.
